newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Fracmaster chief seen selling stake.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Fracmaster chief seen selling stake.

text.p: Oil services firm Canadian Fracmaster Ltd. is expected to announce as early as Wednesday that Chairman Alfred Balm will sell all or most of his majority stake, valued at about C$550 million ($396 million), on the open market, industry sources said.
"You're right bang on the money," one well-placed source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters on Tuesday when posed with the scenario.
Fracmaster officials were not immediately available for comment.

Balm owns about 67 percent of the outstanding shares of Calgary-based Fracmaster, which provides high-tech oil well cementing, fracturing and coiled tubing services in the North American energy sector and takes oil in return for well stimulation services in Russian joint ventures.
It also performs a growing number of fee-for-service well operations in Russia.

At Fracmaster's current share price of C$19.25 ($13.86) on the Toronto Stock Exchange, Balm's holding would be worth about C$550 million ($396 million). The sale of his majority stake would be a major boost to the marketability of the company's shares.
It was not known, however, whether the Geneva-based businessman, who is also Fracmaster's chief executive, would part with his entire holding or a major portion.

Balm's majority stake in Fracmaster has long been a source of speculation in Canada's oil service and supply industry, which has benefited in the past year from booming Canadian drilling and production activity.

Fracmaster last week reported a 90 percent jump in second-quarter earnings to C$8 million ($5.7 million) or C19 cents (14 cents) a share from year earlier C$4.5 million ($3.2 million) or C10 cents (7 cents) a share.

The company, buoyed by rising revenue in its North American businesses and an improving fiscal and operating climate in Russia, has seen its stock price climb since October to its highest levels since it went public in 1993.
Fracmaster stock sank as low as C$4.70 ($3.38) in late 1995 amid uncertainty over Russia's oil scene.
Company officials took the unusual step in Fracmaster's earnings release last week to to quell employee rumors that the company was set to be taken over.
Chief Financial Officer Gary Sherkey told Reuters at the time that Balm was not in negotiations to sell the company and that the rising share price reflected rosy business fundamentals.
